title: Want a U.S. Visa Interview in Ten Days? That Will Be $750, Please.
excerpt: The State Department will let B1/B2 visa applicants pay their way to the front of the queue starting July 1. For an Indian family of four, the total visa bill could top ₹3 lakh.
body:
The U.S. State Department has announced a pilot programme that will allow visitor visa applicants to pay an additional $750 to secure an interview appointment within ten business days. The service launches on July 1 and runs through December 31, 2026.

The premium fee comes on top of the existing $185 application fee for B1/B2 visas, bringing the total cost to approximately $935 per applicant — or roughly ₹80,000 at current exchange rates. For a family of four, the total visa application bill could approach $3,740, or about ₹3.2 lakh, before a single flight ticket is booked.

## How It Works

Under a Temporary Final Rule published in the Federal Register on June 9, applicants at designated U.S. embassies and consulates will be able to purchase what the State Department calls a "premium appointment service." The fee guarantees an interview slot within ten business days of payment — no written justification required, no need to navigate the existing Priority Appointment Request or referral process.

The programme is being pitched as a "proof-of-concept" pilot. The State Department expects approximately 25,700 applicants per year to use the service, generating an estimated $19.3 million in annual revenue.

Participating embassies and consulates have not yet been announced but are expected to be published before the July 1 launch date. Given that India accounts for the largest volume of B1/B2 visa applications globally, posts in New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Kolkata are widely expected to be included.

## Why It Matters for Indian Travellers

Wait times for U.S. visitor visa interviews at Indian consulates currently range from a few weeks to several months, depending on the post and the season. The backlog has deepened under the current administration's expanded screening requirements, which now include mandatory social media reviews for all H-1B and H-4 applicants — a process that has cascaded into longer wait times across all visa categories.

For business travellers who need to attend a conference or close a deal on short notice, the fee may be a worthwhile investment. For families planning vacations or visiting relatives, the calculus is less clear. The $750 is non-refundable and does not guarantee visa approval — only a faster interview slot.

Immigration attorney Michael Cataliotti told USA Today that the fee is "a lot of money in this country" and "an exorbitant amount in many of the countries where people are applying for these visas."

## Context: A String of New Costs

The premium appointment fee is the latest in a series of cost increases and new charges imposed on foreign nationals seeking to enter the United States. Earlier this year, the State Department began requiring $15,000 bonds from visa applicants in countries with high overstay rates. A separate $250 "visa integrity fee" has also been proposed.

The administration has separately introduced the "Trump Gold Card," which offers permanent residency and a path to citizenship for $1 million.

Meanwhile, the $100,000 H-1B surcharge — Trump's most aggressive visa pricing measure — was struck down by a federal judge on June 9 as an unlawful tax. The administration has said it will appeal.

The combined effect of these policies is a U.S. immigration system that is increasingly pay-to-play, with the wealthiest applicants gaining access to expedited processing while others face lengthening queues and growing uncertainty.

The State Department has emphasised that the premium service is optional and will not affect the regular appointment process. But critics argue that creating a fast lane inevitably degrades the standard lane, as embassy resources are redirected toward premium clients.

The pilot will be reviewed at the end of the year. If demand is strong, a permanent version could follow.

*Sources: U.S. Federal Register Temporary Final Rule (June 9, 2026); State Department; Reuters; USA Today; Washington Examiner*
